title: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) & Shield Ulcers
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the 'Spring Catarrh'—a chronic, bilateral, IgE and T-cell mediated ocular surface inflammation primarily affecting young males in warm climates. This infographic details the spectrum of disease from giant papillae to the sight-threatening shield ulcer.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a severe, recurrent, bilateral allergic inflammation of the ocular surface. It is considered a hybrid hypersensitivity reaction, involving both Type I (IgE-mediated) and Type IV (cell-mediated/Th2) pathways. Characteristically affecting children and young adults, it follows a seasonal pattern (peaking in spring/summer) but can become perennial in tropical environments.

branches: Type I Hypersensitivity: IgE + Mast Cell Degranulation
Type IV Hypersensitivity: Th2 Lymphocyte Activation

rows: Giant papillae (>1mm), 'Cobblestone' appearance, mucus in crevices.
Most severe form; combined features of both types.

sections.title: Symptom Checklist
content: Intense Itching (Pruritus) - Hallmark symptom
Photophobia (often severe)
Thick, ropy, 'stringy' mucoid discharge
Foreign body sensation
Lacrimation and blepharospasm
Burning sensation and heaviness of lids

sections.title: Classic Ocular Signs
content: Giant Papillae: Flattened tops, >1mm diameter on upper tarsus.
Maxwell-Lyons Sign: Fibrin-coated papillae (milky appearance).
Horner-Trantas Dots: Collections of eosinophils and epithelial debris at the limbus.
Pseudo-gerontoxon: Lipid deposit resembling arcus senilis adjacent to limbal inflammation.
Conjunctival Hyperpigmentation: Common in dark-skinned individuals.

rows: Translucent/Opaque plaque covering the ulcer base.
Requires debridement or intensive topical management.
Extensive, thick, elevated plaque with heavy mucus.
Adults (20-50y), history of eczema, inferior tarsal involvement, skin lichenification.
History of contact lens wear, ocular prosthesis, or exposed sutures.
No giant papillae, primarily chemosis and watery discharge, mild cornea involvement.
Superior scarring (Arlt's line), Herbert's pits, non-seasonal.

sections.title: Stepwise Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Conservative: Cold compresses, lubricated eye drops (preservative-free), allergen avoidance.
Step 2: Prophylaxis: Mast cell stabilizers (e.g., Sodium Cromoglicate 2%) or dual-action agents (Olopatadine 0.1% BID).
Step 3: Acute Flare: Topical Steroids (Fluorometholone or Loteprednol for mild; Prednisolone 1% or Dexamethasone for severe).
Step 4: Steroid-Sparing: Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (Cyclosporine A 0.05-1.0% or Tacrolimus 0.03-0.1% ointment).
Step 5: Systemic (Rare): Oral Montelukast or Omalizumab (anti-IgE) in refractory cases.

sections.title: Surgical Management of Shield Ulcer
content: 1. Mechanical Debridement: Removing the macro-plaque from the base.
2. Superficial Keratectomy: Removing calcified or fibrotic plaque material.
3. Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT): To promote re-epithelialization.
4. Botulinum Toxin induced ptosis: (Rarely) to protect the ocular surface.

sections.title: Diagnostic & Monitoring Tools
content: Conjunctival Scraping: Presence of eosinophils (highly suggestive).
Corneal Topography: Mandatory screen for Keratoconus (high association due to rubbing).
AS-OCT: To monitor corneal thickness and shield ulcer depth.
IOP Monitoring: Crucial during steroid therapy (Steroid Responders).

sections.title: URGENT: Red Flags
content: Sudden drop in visual acuity (Shield ulcer/Microbial keratitis)
Rising Intraocular Pressure (IOP) during steroid use
Central corneal thinning or hydrops (Keratoconus progression)
Purulent discharge (Secondary bacterial infection)
Cataract formation (Posterior Subcapsular)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: VKC is usually self-limiting after puberty, but permanent damage occurs during the active years.
Supratarsal steroid injection (Triamcinolone) is highly effective for recalcitrant giant papillae.
Always check for associated Keratoconus; constant eye rubbing is a major risk factor.
Tacrolimus 0.03% skin ointment (applied to lids or off-label in fornix) is a game-changer for steroid-dependent cases.
Shield ulcers are sterile but highly susceptible to secondary bacterial infection.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Cequa/Ikervis: Higher concentration Cyclosporine formulations for faster relief.
Biologicals: Ongoing trials for Dupilumab in severe VKC.
VEGF Inhibitors: Research into reducing limbal neovascularization in chronic cases.
